items.paragraph: Collectors who travelled villages writing down folk songs are usually praised for saving a heritage that would otherwise have vanished. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.

options.A: Since old offenders cannot be reformed, punishment for crimes discovered decades later should aim instead at deterring others from committing similar acts.

items.paragraph: When a crime is discovered decades after it was committed, it is sometimes said that punishing the offender now punishes a different person: the frail old man in the dock shares a name with the young man who did the deed, but little else. The objection has force where punishment is meant to reform, for a person who has long since changed has nothing left to reform. It has less force where punishment is meant to answer the wrong itself, to affirm that the victim mattered and that the act was not acceptable. For that purpose what matters is not whether the offender has changed but whether he is the one responsible, and a change of character, however real, does not transfer responsibility to someone else. Time may therefore weaken some reasons for punishment while leaving others intact.

items.paragraph: Software that anyone may copy, change and share for free poses an obvious puzzle for economics. (1) Thousands of skilled programmers contribute to such projects without being paid by them, and the results compete with products built by firms that charge for theirs. (2) Part of the answer is that many contributors are in fact paid, by employers who depend on the software and find it cheaper to improve a shared tool than to build a private one. (3) For her, the rewards are of a different kind: the pleasure of solving a problem, the respect of peers who can see exactly what she did, and a public record of skill that later employers may value. The last of these rewards is the most economic, and it depends on openness itself, since a contribution hidden inside a firm's private code would be visible to no one outside it. (4) The puzzle is partly dissolved, then, by noticing that open work produces a currency of reputation that closed work cannot.

items.paragraph: The roots of most land plants are joined to fungi that extend far into the soil, trading water and minerals for sugars that the plant makes in its leaves. (1) Because a single fungus can connect to several plants at once, some writers have described forests as communities in which trees share food and warnings through an underground network. (2) What remains uncertain is how much moves, how often, and whether the movement benefits the receiving plant rather than the fungus that carries it. (3) A fungus is not a public utility; it is an organism with interests of its own, and it may move sugar wherever it gains most from doing so. Describing it as a channel for cooperation between trees may therefore attribute to the trees a purpose that belongs, if to anyone, to the fungus. (4) None of this makes the network less remarkable; it makes the question of who is helping whom more interesting than the popular story allows.

items.paragraph: We commonly say that people who work hard deserve their success, and the claim seems hardest to dispute when the success is the reward of visible effort. (1) A surgeon who trained for many years, or a musician who has practised every morning since childhood, appears to have earned whatever recognition follows. (2) If the willingness to persevere is partly a matter of luck, then success built on it is not purely earned either. This does not show that nobody deserves anything, for the argument, pushed far enough, would leave no room for praise or blame of any kind. (3) What it shows is narrower: claims of desert should be made with some humility, since nobody chose all the conditions of their own diligence. (4) Gratitude, on this view, is as fitting a response to one's success as pride.

options.A: Polite formulas are valuable chiefly because they let people conceal contempt and keep strangers at a distance, which allows social life to continue without open conflict.
options.B: Polite formulas are social gestures rather than reports of feeling, so calling them insincere misjudges them, although they can be misused to keep distance or hide contempt.
options.C: No courteous expression can ever be insincere, since the meaning of every polite phrase lies wholly in social routine and never in the feelings of the speaker.
options.D: Because routine courtesies seldom express what speakers really feel, people ought to keep such phrases for occasions on which their words match their inner states.

items.paragraph: Critics of everyday courtesy often complain that phrases such as 'how are you' or 'thank you so much' are empty, since the speaker rarely wants a medical report and is seldom overwhelmed with gratitude. The complaint assumes that words are sincere only when they report an inner state. But many polite formulas are not reports at all; they are moves in a shared routine, closer to a handshake than to a confession. Their meaning lies in being offered and returned, and their omission is noticed precisely because nobody expects them to carry personal feeling. To call them insincere is therefore to judge them by a standard they never claimed to meet. This does not mean that every courteous word is innocent: a formula can be used to hold someone at a distance or to cover contempt. Yet that misuse is possible only because the routine itself has a recognised social meaning.

options.A: Vaccination should be compulsory for everyone who can safely receive it, since those who decline borrow safety from others, including infants and patients who cannot be vaccinated.
options.B: Everyone who stays unvaccinated in a well-vaccinated community is a free rider, since each of them benefits from protection created by neighbours who accepted the burden of vaccination.
options.C: Since community immunity protects people who are not vaccinated, an individual's choice to decline a vaccine has little effect on others and remains a private matter.

items.paragraph: When most of a community is vaccinated against a contagious disease, the few who are not are protected too, because the infection struggles to find a path to them. This makes refusal look costless to the refuser, and some ethicists describe the unvaccinated as free riders on the efforts of others. The label is apt for some and unjust to others. It fits a person who could safely be vaccinated and declines because others have made the risk small, since that person's safety is borrowed from neighbours who accepted the minor burden. It does not fit an infant too young for the vaccine or a patient whose treatment rules it out; for them, the protection of the crowd is not a free ride but the only protection available, and it is precisely the reason the rest of us have to keep it intact.
